oai_dc:dc.dc:description: L’actualité en matière d’éthique environnementale conduit l’auteure de cette recension plus loin qu’il n’est d’usage en la matière. Outre le présent ouvrage, un colloque « Ecosophies : la philosophie à l’épreuve de l’écologie », qui a récemment eu lieu à la Cité des sciences et de l’industrie1 montre l’intérêt des universitaires français pour l’éthique environnementale. Il est vrai que s’est développée aux Etats-Unis, en Australie, en Allemagne et dans les pays scandinaves une réflexion morale sur les rapports de l’homme à son environnement naturel et que la France et les nations latines sont demeurées à l’écart de ce mouvement qu’elles assimilent à une tentative « libérale » ou « réactionnaire » de saper les universaux issus des Lumières et les droits imprescriptibles de la personne humaine (alors que certains courants de l’éthique environnementale accordent des droits à la nature la dotant de valeur intrinsèque). Cependant, ce rejet n’est pas définitif d’autant plus que les travaux issus de ces traditions sont désormais mieux connus et accessibles en français (Éthique de l'environnement, textes réunis et présentés par Hicham-Stéphane Afeissa, Paris, Vrin, 2007) ; il est possible que l’appel croissant aux individus et à leur conscience dans le cadre des politiques publiques environnementales joue sur la manière de concevoir le rôle d’une éthique environnementale. En effet, dans divers secteurs de l’environnement, où il s’agit de protéger des biens communs, de limiter l’endommagement, la dégradation voire la destruction des ressources, il est de plus en plus fait appel à la responsabilité des différents acteurs sociaux, citoyens compris, dans le cadre de la mise en place des politiques publiques. D’une action normative et contraignante imposée par l’Etat, on passe progressivement à la recherche d’une « gouvernance collaborative, reposant davantage sur des mécanismes incitatifs, contractuels et concertés ».Le présent compte-rendu d’ouvrage offre l’opportunité d’un bref état des lieux et des forces en présence en France et aux Etats-Unis qui, l’espère t-on, peut être utile au lecteur. La conclusion présentera des pistes de réflexion.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Formation par la perturbation : effets sur les préoccupations et l’apprentissage collectif à partir de l’expérience vécue
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This study analyses the effects of a perturbation-based simulation training programme, focusing on individual concerns and collective learning processes that emerge during the activity. Analysis of the experiences of three learners highlights the heterogeneity of these experiences and the differentiated effects of disruption on individual activity. These differences nevertheless foster collective adaptation through mutual adjustments and the mobilisation of socio-affective dimensions. Our results show that these localised effects are useful indicators allowing trainers to regulate learners’ activity during simulation. Furthermore, the study highlights the emergence of collective learning processes described in the literature (sharing, reflexivity, co-construction), and an original process, that of the protection of the collective, defined as the spontaneous response to an event threatening the continuity of collective activity. This process contributes to the reconfiguration of the activity and to the development of a collective awareness of the situation, which is conducive to adaptation in complex and uncertain contexts. These results highlight the value of perturbation simulation in enriching collective learning.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Former à soigner autrement ? Analyse didactique d’une démarche low‑tech de simulation en santé
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In view of the growing contribution of healthcare systems to ecosystem degradation, training institutions are increasingly called upon to rethink their pedagogical practices, particularly in simulation-based education. This article examines the emergence of low-tech approaches in health simulation as an alternative to the dominant paradigm based on high technologization and realistic reproduction of clinical environments. Building on prior work addressing the ecological impact of healthcare systems and sustainability initiatives developed in certain simulation centers, the article identifies the core principles structuring a low-tech approach across four dimensions: usefulness, durability, accessibility, and appropriation. Through a case study illustrative of an institutional culture oriented toward sustainability, the analysis focuses on the activity of designing a wound simulation model, drawing on the theoretical contributions of professional didactics. The article concludes by framing simulation as a space for pedagogical and institutional experimentation, within which more frugal and sustainable forms of care-related activity can be envisioned.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Développer le potentiel constructif des simulations de crise : leçons d’une série d’analyses de l’activité
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article analyzes ways to enhance the constructive potential of crisis simulations, starting from the observation that traditional formats, often standardized and repetitive, offer limited opportunities for learning and performance improvement. Based on a series of studies conducted in real-world contexts using methods of activity and participant experience analysis, we propose three design principles aimed at fostering the constructive potential of these simulations: designing them (i) as spaces for controlled experimentation or (ii) as spaces for immersed reflexivity, and (iii) integrating participatory design elements. We then specify the overarching conditions required to implement these principles, encapsulated in the concept of “good enough simulations”. Finally, we outline promising research directions derived from our findings.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Les compromis dans l’activité : comprendre les logiques de production et de protection pour agir en prévention
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This paper looks at the notion of compromise in relation to exposure to silica dust in the construction industry. Exposure to this chemical raise questions about the activities of the workers exposed. The ergotoxicological approach to work activity reveals that, in order to achieve production objectives, these workers make various forms of compromise in situations of exposure to chemical substances. The aim of this paper is to highlight the different forms of compromise involved in such exposure. To this end, the methodology used takes inspiration from the work activity analysis approach in ergonomics and, more specifically, from the classic approaches used in ergotoxicology to understand exposure to chemical substances and to transform situations of occupational exposure to chemicals. The results highlight first of all the compromises between protection and production logics, and secondly the compromises within the protection logics themselves. The compromises between protection and production logics are discussed in several ergotoxicology studies. These compromises are highlighted by analysing the factors that determine them. These are technical/material, human and organisational determinants. One of the main contributions of our work concerns the visibility of the compromises made within the protection logics themselves. On the basis of these results, we discuss the notion of compromise and its potential contribution to solving the enigma of exposure to chemicals. Our results also allow us to question the use of this notion to move towards a constructed safety and development of the activity of workers exposed to chemicals.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Former à la gestion de crise par la simulation : réflexions à partir d’un modèle de l’activité d’adaptation pour gérer les risques dans différents types de situation de crise
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Crisis management is a complex activity that involves numerous challenges, including during the activity of crisis units. Scientific literature still offers relatively few models to help us understand these challenges—models that might nonetheless provide a relevant foundation for developing the ability of operators to manage crisis situations. This article aims to address this limitation by combining two perspectives: the modeling of operator activity in crisis situations, and the design of simulation-based training. We first describe the foundations of the model, then present it in detail. The model subsequently allows us to formulate avenues for reflection on simulation-based training for risk management across various types of crisis situation. In concrete terms, it involves an articulation between general (adaptation, transformation, progression) and specific principles (unique to each type of crisis situation). This approach aims to enhance the relevance and effectiveness of simulations, thereby fostering the development of adaptative activity to manage risks in different types of crisis situation.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: La conception en situation comme un bricolage : conduire des microprojets dans les plateformes pétrolières
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This paper analyzes how certain operations carried out by operators working on offshore oil platforms cope with operational variability and uncertainties by implementing a situated design akin to bricolage. Based on Ergonomic Work Analysis (EWA), we conducted research focused on the activity of teams responsible for moving loads on “Floating Production, Storage and Offloading” (FPSO) platforms in Brazil. The analysis shows that the operators are conducting 'micro-projects', which mobilize bricolage thinking to carry out their tasks. Two types of microproject are identified: one takes place prior to the effectuation of action and allows the design of a load-moving system, the other is carried out during the action and aims to resolve unforeseen operational events. These microprojects are of an ephemeral nature, well-suited to a specific context. In conclusion, the article highlights the importance of microprojects understood as adaptive resources that allow operators to effectively manage the complex and unpredictable situations they face. It advocates integrating this understanding into the design of work systems, in order to improve the autonomy, efficiency and safety of the daily operational challenges they face.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Douleurs chroniques et limitations fonctionnelles après un accident : la reprise de l’activité aux confluents d’une mobilisation de stratégies personnelles et des acquis de la réadaptation
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: When an accident is severe in terms of injuries, it can have multiple consequences, including the onset of pain and functional limitations. Adomino effect takes place, affecting the activities of daily life and leading people to reinvent themselves in order to establish some degree of continuity with their previous lives. The aim of this article, based on semi-structured interviews and observations of vocational workshops with people undergoing rehabilitation with a vocational component following an orthopaedic trauma, is to explore the strategies they used to resume their activities. The analyses, carried out by an interdisciplinary team comprised of anthropologists, a sociologist, physiotherapists, a psychologist, and a doctor specialising in rehabilitation, show that, prior to their participation in the programme, these people developed personalised strategies for carrying out the activity, taking into account their physical limitations and while managing their pain. Subsequently, the rehabilitation stay provided access to new learning, thereby helping to strengthen skills and sometimes challenging previous experiential knowledge. The knowledge, advice and tools acquired during rehabilitation strengthened their ability to adapt to the situation and encouraged them to resume or better manage their activity, although these effects did not systematically translate into effective professional reintegration, due to factors related to their state of health or to the professional reintegration system in general.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: L’activité entrepreneuriale des artisans du bâtiment : définir une configuration productive, entre soutenabilité du travail et durabilité économique
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article focuses on how building tradespeople create and define the characteristics of their company, beyond the diversity of the construction projects they carry out. Tradespeople are self-employed workers (just like the liberal professions or farmers). But the building trade is a specific socio-professional configuration, which remains relatively misunderstood despite its economic importance. Our objective is to examine the “company” as an object that building tradespeople define and design in their activity. We propose to use the term “entrepreneurial activity” to characterize the activity they engage in to create and maintain their business over the long term. And we seek to understand the latter using the concept of “productive configuration”, the dimensions of which we discuss in our article. We show that the productive configuration has a significant impact on the economic sustainability of the company, but also on the working conditions of the tradespeople. In particular it is the coherence that the tradesman is able to give to this productive configuration that is decisive. And maintaining this coherence is a long-term task: it is especially destabilized by the hiring of an employee. This event calls into question not only the productive configuration, but also the role that tradespeople play. However, despite the challenges of entrepreneurial activity, most building tradespeople base the creation or takeover of their business solely on their technical expertise. In this context, these entrepreneurs are ill-prepared for the creation or takeover of a business, the outcome of which is therefore uncertain.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Appréhender la territorialisation d’un système soutenable de travail. Réflexions à partir de l’exemple des systèmes alimentaires territorialisés
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The analysis of work carried out by actors involved in food system transitions in the context of territorialized public action within a territorial food project, with a view to developing their sustainability, presented us with four conceptual challenges. We propose a specific analytical framework, based on three complementary fields of research (rural sociology, political sociology, and transition studies). This framework is built to understand: what is involved in the processes of transition to sustainable and territorialized food systems, who is involved in these processes, and the coordination required. We present this framework to establish what we believe to be the most appropriate focus for the analysis: the coupling of the work system with its environment. We then illustrate how we conducted the analysis and the results that emerged at the level of a research project. In the final section, we draw some lessons to highlight the theoretical, methodological, and pragmatic issues that we believe still need to be addressed to analyze and support, as ergonomists, systemic transformations with a view to contributing to the development of sustainable work systems

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Mettre en espace la transition. Retour sur la construction d’un dispositif participatif pour la planification énergétique territoriale
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: France’s national energy transition strategy aims to achieve carbon neutrality by 2050. This target requires both ambitious reductions in energy consumption and a significant increase in renewable energy production. These objectives are set within a context of decentralized public energy action, placing local authorities at the heart of a dual challenge: technical (how to consume and produce energy sustainably at the territorial level?) and democratic (how to conduct the transition in a way that is perceived as legitimate by residents?). The high level of conflict surrounding the spatial implementation of the transition—particularly the deployment of renewable energy infrastructure—calls for a rethinking of public participation in decisions related to territorial energy governance. In this context, energy planning (notably through the development of documents such as the Territorial Climate-Air-Energy Plans, PCAET) can be seen as a privileged space for democratizing public policies on energy transition. As a comprehensive and coherent territorial project, energy planning offers an opportunity to engage residents in the democratic shaping of these policies. This article explores this hypothesis by presenting an ethnographic study of the construction of a participatory device designed to involve residents of a Pôle d’Équilibre Territorial et Rural (PETR) with 80,000 inhabitants in spatializing the energy objectives defined in its PCAET. As a member of the TEPOS network (Territories with Positive Energy), the PETR aims to meet its energy needs through local renewable sources. The device under study centers on a digital platform inviting contributors to propose actions for mapping, on a territorial map, the community’s targets for renewable energy production and consumption management. Our analysis draws on observations and interviews conducted during an ongoing process at the time of writing. Rather than describing the final state of the device as envisioned by its promoters, we focus on key points of arbitration that emerged among the actors involved—points that reveal the inherent difficulties of democratizing energy planning issues. First, it appears that the spatial planning exercise itself (whether participatory or not) is subject to strong constraints of various kinds (regulatory, budgetary, political, and material), which limit the community’s room for maneuver in achieving its TEPOS objectives. Second, the narrowness of this room for maneuver raises questions about the meaning of participation: how can a device be designed that offers residents a real, concrete, and understandable political outlet for their engagement? Third, the massive scale of the efforts required (in terms of renewable energy production and consumption reduction) makes it difficult for individuals to grasp planning at the territorial level. Our investigation ultimately suggests—and this is its main finding—that the very idea of participatory energy planning faces a paradox: while its purpose is to prevent local conflicts over renewable energy infrastructure by involving residents in defining the energy transition at the territorial level, the limited room for maneuver of local authorities, combined with the massive scale of the efforts required, tends to reduce participation to an exercise in raising awareness or acculturating residents to a reality that is imposed upon them.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: School–Community Councils as Political Spaces in Decentralized Educational Governance in Brazil
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article analyzes School–Community Councils (CECs) as institutionalized political spaces within the framework of the decentralization of educational governance in Brazil. Under the federal program “Direct Money to Schools Program” (PDDE), which transfers resources directly to schools, the CECs serve as local bodies responsible for managing and ensuring accountability for public funds.Situated within debates in the political geography of democracy and participatory governance, the article conceptualizes these councils as relational and situated spaces where negotiation, deliberation, conflict, and political learning take place. The analysis draws on research conducted in eleven municipal schools in Niterói (State of Rio de Janeiro), based on documentary examination of financial reports and meeting minutes, as well as interviews and questionnaires with council members.The findings show that despite a homogeneous institutional framework, the CECs exhibit differentiated configurations of participation and accountability. While dynamics of political learning can be observed, the relationship between democratic management, resource oversight, and the improvement of educational services remains complex and non-linear.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Entre approche critique et opérationnelle, quelle dialectique ? Retour sur le rôle d’agent intermédiaire de la géographie politique de l’énergie
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article explores the complex role of social science researchers acting as advisory partners and intermediary agent within European energy transition frameworks. Specifically, it examines the SIreNERGY project (Interreg Europe), which aims to foster Renewable Energy Sources (RES) in rural areas through the lenses of social acceptance and citizen participation. The research focuses on a central tension: how can political geography maintain its critical edge while being "enrolled" to provide operational tools for public policy practitioners?Research positioning and theoretical frameworkThe study is situated at the intersection of political geography, political ecology, and transition studies. Historically, geography has oscillated between being a “service to power” and a tool for radically criticizing the system. In the context of the climate crisis, the European Union increasingly requires citizen participation and social acceptance as prerequisites for energy projects. However, many researchers fear that these concepts are used superficially. Instead of giving real power to citizens, they sometimes simply serve to make people accept projects imposed from above (acceptance management). The authors of this article position themselves as intermediary agents. This position is not understood as a neutral, technical transfer, but as a political act of translation. Their goal is to translate complex theories (i.e. power inequalities, energy justice,…) into operational tools without diluting their critical substance.Methodology: embedded reflexivity and “tiny tools”The methodology relies on an embedded research posture, focused on participant observation. The empirical material consists of: (i) Two Holistic Diagnostics conducted across five EU regions (Spain/Basque Country, Sweden, Poland, Romania, Bulgaria) to map energy profiles and social perceptions; (ii) Two surveys, through common questionnaires tracking changes in partners’ perceptions; (iii)Collective workshops, using “tiny tools” – i.e. simplified analytical frameworks to encourage practitioners to reflect on their own power dynamics; (iv) Cartographic visualization translating qualitative social data into interactive maps to facilitate multi-stakeholder dialogue.Main resultsThe findings of this research highlight the challenges faced by political geography when it is “enrolled” into energy transition programs. By acting as intermediaries, this article identified three main types of results: (i) Methodological reduction and instrumentalization: To make critical concepts accessible, researchers provided clear frameworks, but risked reducing the depth of the critique. This led to a paradox: while tools helped partners move beyond simple information-sharing, many still viewed “social mentality” or “lack of trust” as the primary barriers, rather than questioning the socio-political structures of the projects themselve. (ii) The balance between objectivity and prescription: The researcher’s role oscillated between being a neutral observer (objectification) and an active advisor (prescription). Because citizen participation remained marginal, the researchers stepped out of their neutral posture to promote the “Energy Community” model. However, this created a gap between the EU’s “ideal” model and local realities where such initiatives were misunderstood or absent. (3) The structural limits of “enrolled” geography: The study identifies spatial limits (the gap between European literature and local histories, such as the suspicion toward cooperatives in post-communist contexts); temporal limits (the short timeframe of Interreg prevents long-term follow-up of how tools are used); and action limits (being “close to power” favors energy deployment over challenging transition goals).

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Légalisera, légalisera pas ? Stratégies face à la construction illégale du barrage de Caussade : entre anti-ZAD, bataille judiciaire et politique du laisser-faire
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Controversial water storage projects have been at the center of media attention due to environmental mobilisations. In the case of the Caussade reservoir (Lot-et-Garonne), while associations opposed to its construction have worked on the judicial front, the project's supporters opted for visible modes of action in the field and in the press with the illegal construction of a dam. The article analyses discourses based on 395 press citations to understand the strategies of involved stakeholders and their evolution between 2016 and 2024. The paper first positions the research within the controversies over water storage, presents the case study, and then the methodology based on a statistical and qualitative analysis of discourses. Finally, the results show the surprise created by the rapid establishment of an "anti- Zone to Defend" and the construction of the dam by the project's supporters. This, thereby limited the modes of action of the project's opponents to judicial actions. Furthermore, the temporal evolution of these positions highlights how the illegality of the reservoir paradoxically allows the French state to maintain an ambiguous position regarding the water storage project.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Spatialisation des perceptions de l’évolution d’un territoire suite à la fermeture d’une centrale nucléaire
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This contribution proposes to revisit the experience of the closure of the Fessenheim nuclear power plant (France). It questions the notions of energy and territorial transitions and their representations by the habitants. The hypothesis is that the dismantling of a power plant can be the starting point of a disruptive and radical break to embark on a new trajectory for the territory. We rely on the results of a field study which aims to reveal the place of a nuclear power in the discourses of the inhabitants of the territory after the closure. To do this, we are deploying the Perception-Based Regional Mapping (PBRM), which is carried out through cartographic interviews. This method collecting information through maps and reveals spontaneous representations of post-dismantling issues. The question is whether the closure of the plant can be, or not, an accelerator for the reconversion of the territory or whether dependence on nuclear activity hinders the possibility of envisaging other trajectories (industrial or not). This study highlights the challenges of spontaneously emerging representations of space and the gap between the political will to decarbonize the territory. It gives visibility to the agricultural subject in a territory classically identified as nuclear. This contrast is particularly notable and highlights an ability of the inhabitants to go beyond the strong nuclear identity of the Fessenheim territory, which is perhaps not unrelated to the shutdown of the plant itself.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Une transition énergétique « géopolitique » ? Le rôle de la Commission européenne dans la réponse européenne à la crise de l’énergie (2021-2023)
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The aim of this article is to examine the European Commission's political action during the energy crisis (2021–2023) by focusing on conflicts between actors regarding the appropriate geographical scale for responding to this crisis. While the first few months of the crisis may have encouraged some EU member states to prioritise national energy policies, the European Commission quickly intervened to use the crisis as a new milestone for EU institutions' political action in the field of energy through the REPowerEU plan. The article questions this position taken by the Commission, both in its official statements and in the instruments proposed in 2022, with the aim of examining the influence of the crisis in the ongoing implementation of European energy governance as part of the European Union’s policy action to achieve infrastructure integration, market liberalisation and energy transition in line with the EU's climate objectives. This article contributes to the field of European integration studies by examining the instruments and discourse of the REPowerEU plan as a new phase in the integration of national energy policies at the EU level. The literature on European integration offers multiple explanations for this process. Some scholars, adopting a neo-functionalist perspective, highlight the expansion of EU institutional powers (Maltby, 2013), while others, from an intergovernmental perspective, emphasize the persistent influence of Member States (Thaler, 2016). Although the progressive integration of energy policies at the EU level is widely acknowledged, it occurs in a context where the division of competences between EU institutions and Member States remains unstable (Szulecki & Westphal, 2018 ; Herranz-Surrallés et al., 2020) and primarily manifests through evaluation and oversight mechanisms within EU institutions (Knodt & Schoenefeld, 2020; Bocquillon & Maltby, 2020). Consequently, energy integration at the EU level is a hybrid process, shaped by consensus-building between Member States and EU institutions, where competing rational interests and divergent policy framings often clash (Schmidt, 2020).This article considers the European energy crisis as a case study for analysing the Commission's role in a specific institutional and geographical environment. It consists of an interpretative approach to the Commission's role during the crisis and its impact on strengthening the European energy scale. It is based on EU legislation and official documentation, a dozen semi-structured interviews with officials from the Directorate-General for Energy conducted between December 2023 and February 2024, and three months of participant observation between March and June 2023 within the same directorate.This article finds that, despite opposition from certain states, particularly in Eastern Europe, which advocate a national approach to energy policies, the Commission has mostly succeeded in making the European scale the main scale for European energy policies in response to the crisis. This development should be seen in the context of a strengthening of the European scale in the energy field, recently through the regulation on energy governance in the Union. The response to the energy crisis has contributed to this process, in particular through the adoption of joint procurement AggregateEU and the acceleration of the deployment of energy from renewable sources.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: « Tout a commencé un soir de tempête. » Chroniques géolégales du contentieux énergétique sur l’île de Sein
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article presents a geolegal analysis of a unique energy transition controversy on Sein island in French Brittany, centred on the first-ever rejection of the traditional electricity distribution system in order to propel a faster transition to renewable sources. In 2013, a citizen-owned company challenged the monopoly of the historical operator of the island's electricity concession to end the island's dependence on oil after repeated but unsuccessful requests to the operator since the 1990s. The island of Sein, located off the coast of Finistère, is a non-interconnected zone, which justifies that a single company has an integrated monopoly on energy supply. The citizen-led company sought not only to generate renewable energy but also to secure access to the grid to manage the balance between supply and demand – a crucial challenge given the intermittent nature of renewable energy. Following a refusal from the historical company, tensions escalated and eventually led to an unprecedented legal dispute. The case, which extended far beyond the island's small territory, took on national and European political significance. The dispute became a subversive act, challenging established political and energy models and forcing a renegotiation of powers over the distribution network. The article addresses two questions: how can the scope and intensity of the dispute be explained, and in what ways does law operate as an instrument of power in the implementation of the energy transition? To answer these questions, it builds on a dual theoretical framework that brings the geolegal literature into dialogue with material politics. In doing so, the article contributes to expanding geolegal scholarship toward socio-technical issues such as energy, while also reflecting on how recent geolegal developments invite a renewed and deepened interrogation of law within political geography. Drawing on a fieldwork conducted in the summer of 2024 (comprising 9 interviews and a week of non-participant observation), this paper explores three central tensions in the construction of energy spatialities. First, it argues that the material characteristics of decentralised, intermittent energy reshape strategic control points within energy systems, positioning the shared distribution network and the related balancing of supply and demand as a central site of power struggles - an issue largely unexplored by geographers. Second, the paper highlights the importance of studying the legal frameworks that give rise to new power hierarchies between actors. Finally, from an energy justice perspective, the case calls into question the legitimacy of vertically integrated monopolies and the resistances to centralised governance. The study shows how law and jurisdictional scales become tools for shaping local resistance. By using European law, local actors challenge historically dominant structures. Beyond the French case, Sein Island highlights the strategic nature of multi-scalar energy governance. This complex interplay of interests reveals the power relations that shape the dynamics of energy transitions across Europe and the trade-offs that can emerge from them. The case is particularly significant as it provides a rare example of a major political and regulatory resistance to electrical decentralization. It contributes to debates on energy justice and the transformation of socio-spatial power relations in the transition, while also providing insights into seizing the growing role of law in energy dynamics within political geography.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Le pouvoir des gestionnaires de réseau électrique de gouverner les systèmes électriques insulaires
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: At the core of organizational models of island electricity systems - traditionally based on the centralization of power flows (Coutard, Rutherford, 2009) - lies the grid operator, which is legally required to continuously meet consumer demand by regulating electricity generation (Pilo, 2022). Over the past two decades however, the development of decentralized generation technologies (such as solar photovoltaics and wind power), along with advances in energy storage (including batteries and hydrogen), has challenged this centralized organization and, more broadly, the role of grid operators in electricity governance. By bridging the sociology of translation and the sociology of public action, this article contributes to the analysis of the conditions under which sociotechnical systems exhibit “obduracy” (Hommels, 2005) in the face of the hybridization of electricity services (Furlong, 2014; Lawhon et al., 2018; Jaglin, 2019; Pilo, 2022). The analysis draws on a comparative study of Guadeloupe and Barbados - two non-interconnected island electricity systems in which operators combine generation and distribution functions. It is based on two empirical fieldworks comprising 118 semi-structured interviews with a wide range of stakeholders (grid operators, public authorities, regulators, producers, project developers, users, trade unions, and civil society actors), complemented by the analysis of grey literature and regulatory documents, as well as observation sequences capturing governance processes in practice. The findings highlight three main contributions. First, the article shows that the expansion of renewable energy leads to differentiated trajectories depending on sociopolitical contexts: it may result in forms of system reconfiguration - as in Barbados, where decentralized initiatives are integrated into the grid - or in processes of system rigidification, as illustrated by the conversion of thermal power plants in Guadeloupe. Second, despite these variations, the article shows that the interdependence between actors makes the evolution of electricity systems particularly difficult, especially with regard to centralized transmission infrastructures. This dynamic contributes to a form of “obduracy” of sociotechnical systems (Hommels, 2005), as historically dominant grid operators are able to mobilize significant power resources (Lambelet, Pflieger, 2016) through processes of translation (Callon, 1986). Third, the article highlights the reliance of network operators on multidimensional risk regulation instruments, whose importance is heightened in small, autonomous island systems, thereby revealing the significance of the “material fragility” (Denis, Pontille, 2023) of insular infrastructures.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Pour une géographie politique des espaces fiscaux du nucléaire : une comparaison entre France et États-Unis
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Local tax revenues generated by energy infrastructures and particularly nuclear power plants are frequently portrayed in the literature as mechanisms of economic dependence that lock host communities into path-dependent trajectories, thus hindering energy transitions. Within energy geography and nuclear studies, these fiscal flows are often implicitly treated as instruments of power benefiting operators by securing local acceptability. This article challenges this assumption by repositioning local nuclear taxation within the field of fiscal geography and by explicitly theorizing power relations. Building on Barnett and Duvall’s multidimensional taxonomy of power, the paper asks whether and how fiscal flows associated with nuclear facilities produce coercive, institutional, structural, or productive power over host territories.Empirically, the article develops a comparative analysis of two nuclear power stations embedded in contrasting fiscal and governance systems, Fessenheim in France and Seabrook in the United States. Methodologically, it proposes a two-step approach. First, it reconstructs the “fiscal spaces” generated by each plant by contextualizing relevant monetary flows, including taxes, subsidies, infrastructure investments, and indirect financial contributions. This reconstruction combines quantitative data (local and intermunicipal public accounts, fiscal reports, impact studies) with qualitative material (semi-structured interviews, grey literature, municipal council records, and field observations). Second, these fiscal spaces are analyzed through Barnett and Duvall’s fourfold framework to identify the concrete modalities through which power is exercised in these flows.The results demonstrate that fiscal flows do not generate uniform or automatic dependencies. In Fessenheim, despite high local revenues linked to nuclear taxation, the operator’s coercive and institutional power over local authorities remains limited, as fiscal rules are centrally defined by the state. Power relations are instead shaped by intermunicipal redistribution mechanisms and national compensation schemes, which produce territorial tensions and shifting positions among local actors. In Seabrook, fiscal relations are negotiated locally through property tax assessments, introducing uncertainty and periodic conflict, but also constraining unilateral domination by either the operator or the municipality. Across both cases, productive power operates unevenly through fiscal imaginaries, strongly in France and weakly in the U.S., reflecting differences in operator status and governance scales. By demonstrating that the political effects of fiscal flows depend on legal frameworks, temporalities, scales, and imaginaries, this article argues for moving beyond reductive notions of addictive economies. It shows that understanding energy transitions requires analyzing money not as an intrinsic source of power, but as a relational and spatialized mediator embedded in specific fiscal spaces

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Les gigafactories chinoises dans l’Union européenne : encastrements différenciés et asymétries de souveraineté
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Over the past decade, Chinese companies have taken a central position in the European electric vehicle battery landscape. Their investments in large-scale production sites, often supported by national subsidies and regional development plans, raise fundamental questions about the nature of sovereignty and territorial anchoring in the energy transition. As these infrastructures multiply across the European union (EU), they reveal tensions between industrial ambition and external dependence. This article examines how gigafactories backed by Chinese stakeholders participate in the restructuring of power across EU industrial territories. It treats these factories as production facilities but also as instruments that embed geopolitical influence into material landscapes. They shape norms and standards and stabilise new forms of interdependence. The analysis engages with current research on energy transitions as contested political processes and with critical perspectives on infrastructure as a tool of strategic projection.The study draws from four interconnected literatures. First, political geography provides tools to analyse how infrastructures redistribute authority across space. Second, energy transition research underlines the asymmetries and competing interests shaping low-carbon strategies. Then, critical infrastructure studies show how material systems operate as instruments of power and standardisation. Finally, value chain geography highlights the differentiated territorialisation of global production networks.The research adopts a qualitative and comparative approach. It applies an embedded grid framework to analyse how foreign-led production sites are integrated across four dimensions: productive, normative, institutional, and socio-territorial. This framework is used to examine three battery factories involving Chinese stakeholders, located in Germany, France and Hungary. These selected cases correspond to either operational or under construction projects and having direct links with Chinese companies. Fieldwork conducted between 2024 and 2025 combines document analysis, media sources and semi-structured interviews with public officials, corporate actors and local stakeholders.The findings reveal contrasting modalities of infrastructural embedding. In some cases, industrial integration and public oversight enable strategic coordination, while in others, permissive governance facilitates foreign-led development with limited political framing. Across contexts, Chinese firms consolidate positions within the European battery value chain through technological control and standards diffusion. These processes challenge the coherence of the EU’s claim to industrial autonomy. By analysing gigafactories as situated infrastructures shaped by external power and internal fragmentation, the article contributes to a political geography of the energy transition. It highlights the need to reassess the role of infrastructure in the production of territorial asymmetries. Gigafactories make visible how low-carbon strategies intersect with geopolitical logics and reconfigure the spatial foundations of sovereignty in contemporary Europe.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Le conflit du parc éolien de Fosen Vind en Norvège : interprétations antagonistes des territoires et de la transition énergétique
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the conflict sparked by the development of the Fosen Vind mega-wind farm in Norway on grazing lands used by Sámi populations, the only officially recognized indigenous people in mainland Europe. This conflict has been extensively studied by Norwegian researchers, primarily through the prism of political science, law, postcolonial studies or social psychology. Most of the work on the Fosen Vind conflict uses the concepts of ‘energy transition’ and ‘just transition’ to frame the issue, but with little consideration of how these concepts are used by the various actors involved. We will seek to examine the extent to which competing representations of energy transition clash, adopting a reflexive stance on this polysemic concept, which should not only be seen as an analytical framework, but also as a discursive and political construct. We will analyse this conflict through the prism of the cognitive frameworks employed by the actors involved. We will highlight the territorial dimension of this framework, which mobilises different types of relationships with territories, from living spaces closely linked to identity to global spaces.The article is based on a qualitative methodology. This study draws on a month-long period of fieldwork in Norway carried out by one of the authors in March 2022, which included 14 semi-structured individual interviews with various stakeholders (researchers, members of associations campaigning against wind farm development, associations for the protection of indigenous peoples, residents living near wind farms). Encountering some reticence among the Sámi stakeholders to talk about their long and arduous struggle against several wind farms, we focused on informal discussions and participation in the Sámi Easter festival rather than interviews. This fieldwork was complemented by a discourse analysis based on press articles, official government documents, company reports, and NGO publications. Drawing on several field visits carried out between October 2021 and May 2025 by the other author as well as a detailed analysis of Statkraft's annual reports between 2009 and 2025, the cognitive frameworks used by the project's supporters were brought to light. While it is possible to simplify the issue by dividing the actors into two camps, those opposed to Fosen Vind and those in favour of it, an examination of their motivations and representations reveals very different cognitive frameworks, which interact and evolve throughout the conflict. The territoriality of these different frameworks varies: while the Sámi opponents are defending their traditional territories, which have strong cultural, symbolic and identity value, and some residents are seeking to preserve their residential and recreational areas, certain environmental associations are defending ‘nature’ and its biodiversity, or even the national territory, while more generalist discourses on the climate context and environmental protection refer to global issues. While the concept of energy transition is initially little used by the actors involved, the conflict has given rise to discourse on energy transition and has also helped to structure its definition.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Recursos renovables y minerales, para demandas externas o necesidades locales. Dos fuerzas de la transición energética argentina
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: At the beginning of the 21st century, the transition to a low-carbon energy model, with its opportunities and tensions, modifies the role of fossil fuels in the socio-productive organisation of territories and their hegemony on the global geopolitical scene. The incorporation of peripheral geographies into the global economy through the advancement of new activities and the application of innovative technologies shows the spatial dimension of the transition process (Guibert et al., 2018; Schweitzer, 2016). In Latin America, since the late 20th century, processes have been underway that integrate territories into the international market, with a particular focus on their energy resources. In this region, Argentina—given its availability of land, water, energy, minerals, and other resources—is valued within global accumulation circuits, attracting investment (Vázquez, 2021). Certain regions are valorized by projects that seek to extract strategic minerals, such as lithium, generate electricity and/or produce green hydrogen, taking advantage of available solar and wind resources. The expansion of these energies and the spatial transformations that result from them invite us to rediscover aspects of the relationship between energy and territory. This paper draws on transition studies and energy-territory nexus theories (Bridge and Gailing, 2020; Exner et al., 2015; Hurd et al., 2012; Rothkopf, 2009) to study the energy transition in Argentina from the perspective of the harnessing of strategic renewable and mineral resources, analyzing their contribution to local needs or extraterritorial demands. The paper stems from results of doctoral and postdoctoral research carried out between 2018 and 2025. The research is based on a qualitative methodology and a territorial, multidimensional, and multi-scalar perspective. Initially, documentary analysis was used, including a study of official public documents, a review of national and provincial regulations, and of national and international literature specializing in energy transitions and energy geography. For primary data collection, fieldwork sessions were organized within the framework of collective, interdisciplinary research projects. These sessions involved gathering primary information through on-site observation and semi-structured interviews with key informants at different levels of involvement in the region's energy dynamics. These included managers and technical staff from renewable energy project development companies, investors, electricity distribution companies and cooperatives, public administration officials, civil society actors, non-governmental organizations, and citizens in general. The interviews were structured to identify existing projects, those promoting them, and their objectives. Five main thematic areas were considered to guide the conversation: the genesis and motivation of the initiative; project ownership and financing; actors and stakeholders involved in the project's design and implementation; citizen and local stakeholder involvement; and the intended use of the project's benefits. As part of the main findings, the papers shows that the energy transition in Argentina is driven by two types of processes: one guided by external interests that mobilise resources abroad, exerting a kind of centrifugal force, which serves global value chains and reinforces the country's vocation to satisfy extraterritorial demands; and another, with a centripetal tendency, which emerges from endogenous forces from the territories themselves, seeking to satisfy local needs.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In Colombia, the energy transition implemented since the signing of the Paris Agreement (2015) is reconfiguring the geography of electricity production from renewable energy technologies. This article looks at the installation of industrial solar photovoltaic parks and shows how, by becoming part of the country's existing energy networks, they also enable companies to open up new energy fronts. This process is achieved not only by redefining company-state relations, but also by bringing new private players into the energy market. Drawing on analyses from political ecology, the article shows how the installation of solar panels in the context of the energy transition is ultimately a way of reproducing the logics of land appropriation by large energy companies. However, the article analyzes the opening of new energy fronts not through conflict, but rather by attempting to understand how the energy transition can be sustained across territories. I study the conditions for the implementation of photovoltaic solar panel park infrastructure: which actors contribute to promoting the installation of projects, and what governance, social and political relationships are mobilized.This article is based on several months' fieldwork carried out in Colombia between 2022 and 2024, in several regions: Magdalena medio, Caribean coast and Huila departement. More than 30 interviews, participant observation and a review of governmental and entrepreneurial grey literature (legal documents, company reports, press, social networks) were conducted. In addition, the methodology is based on a cartographic analysis using data from Acolgen, the union of electricity producers in Colombia. This data has been spatialized, enabling me to carry out a cartographic analysis of the opening of new fronts. The results are the followings: new energy fronts are being opened up by solar photovoltaic parks through entrepreneurial projects led by large electricity production companies in Colombia. These companies benefit from favorable legislation and tax advantages granted by the Colombian government. In addition, the government strongly encourages the development of photovoltaic parks. Furthermore, companies rely on the support of cattle ranchers who make their land available for electricity production. As the largest landowners in the region, ranchers are seizing the economic opportunity presented by the energy transition and are taking three types of action: they are selling or leasing their land to companies for the construction of solar farms, or they are partnering with them. It would appear that solar projects are meeting with relatively little opposition from the rest of the population, even though the benefits of the transition are not being widely shared. This is because the region where the farms are being built is historically prone to violence and has been subject to harsh repression in the past. Furthermore, the farms do not cause the direct displacement of residents, which seems to explain the absence of open opposition. However, these farms do not appear to contribute to improving energy justice, as the population does not seem to benefit from better electricity service.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Reducing health inequality from air pollution requires action in deprived-ethnic neighbourhoods: An environmental justice analysis of air quality in England, 2001-2021

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Approaching the spatial dimensions of environmental justice in adaptation policy. The study of flood risk management
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The risk of flooding is increasing as a result of climate change. The unequal social and spatial impact of flooding poses a significant challenge to flood risk management (FRM) policies and raises concerns about environmental justice. This article contributes to the theoretical justice framework by conducting an empirical analysis of FRM policies in four European countries. Drawing on environmental justice literature as well as the framework of FRM strategies, the article demonstrates that fully incorporating spatial justice into FRM is challenging due to the way in which space is framed and narrated. FRM remains dominated by the concept of fixed and hazard-dependent space. The results highlight three dimensions of spatial justice that are often overlooked. Firstly, there is the temporal dimension, referring to the unequal effects that decisions may have on future generations. Secondly, the relational dimension of space refers to the role of social distance from public policy in determining public participation in decision-making processes. Thirdly, the symbolic dimension refers to space as a narrative construction of identity that shapes spatial practices.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Des Lumières chrétiennes ?
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This paper reviews Simon Pietro Calisti’s 2025 book on Voltaire’s Anti-Pascal and its eighteenth-century reception. Calisti treats the Anti-Pascal not as scattered marginalia on Pascal’s Pensées but as the polemical core of a long conflict on the nature of “modernity”: a Voltairian, empiricist and anti-Cartesian naturalisation of the human condition, versus a “Christian modernity” defended by theologians and apologetes who mobilise Cartesian and Malebranchian arguments to reconcile reason and faith. The article highlights Calisti’s analysis of the three waves of Voltaire’s Remarques (1734, 1742 and 1778), the central themes of the quarrel (anthropology, Scripture, deism, Deus absconditus), and the decisive role of the Port-Royal editorial tradition, whose partial cartesianisation of Pascal offers rationalist aguments in favour of the Christian faith. The article then questions the contemporary relevance Calisti assigns to Voltaire’s opponents. Stressing Pascal’s own anti-Cartesian, Gassendist epistemology and the crisis of figurist exegesis after Spinoza and Richard Simon, it argues that eighteenth-century apologetes defend Pascal by abandoning Pascal—either sliding toward deism via metaphysical proofs, toward obscurantist mystery, or toward problematic theological guarantees of certainty. A final regret is Calisti’s omission of Pierre Bayle, whose analyses sharpen the apologetic dilemma and complicate any appeal to “Christian Enlightenment”.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Bilateral asymmetry in the lower limbs in medieval humans and La Ferrassie Neandertals LF1 and LF2
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Bilateral asymmetry in the lower limbs can provide insights into habitual biomechanical loading and mobility patterns in past populations. Previous studies have typically examined lower-limb elements in isolation, potentially overlooking integrated functional signals across the entire limb. Here, we present new data on bilateral asymmetry in medieval humans and the La Ferrassie Neandertals (LF1 and LF2), combining external measurements with cross-sectional biomechanical analyses. We quantified directional (DA) and absolute asymmetry (AA) in femora, tibiae and the first (MT1) and fifth metatarsals (MT5) to evaluate habitual mechanical loading. Medieval humans showed moderate asymmetry in MT1 and the tibia, but no consistent side dominance or inter-element correlations, suggesting substantial individual variation. LF1 and LF2 exhibited higher DA, with distinct patterns between individuals, most likely reflecting adaptation to more intense or repetitive lower-limb loading. Overall, our results highlight individual variability, possible sexual dimorphism and segment-specific adaptation, while underscoring that metatarsal asymmetry in past populations has not been well documented to date. In addition, thanks to high-resolution CT data for LF1 and LF2, our study produced revised and more precise estimates of their biomechanical properties.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: La réception des Pensées de Pascal au Japon : Miki Kiyoshi lecteur du « pari »
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the reception in Japan of Blaise Pascal’s famous “wager” through the interpretation proposed by the philosopher Miki Kiyoshi (1897-1945). While Pascal was initially read in Japan mainly within a religious context, Miki was the first to introduce his work into the field of philosophy proper. Influenced by Heidegger as well as by the Buddhist tradition of Jōdo Shinshū, Miki developed an original existential and religious interpretation of the Pensées, focusing in particular on Pascal’s wager. This article first reconstructs Miki’s intellectual and biographical background, emphasizing his reflections on death, anxiety, and contingency as fundamental dimensions of human existence. It then examines his engagement with Jules Lachelier’s critique of the wager, which rejected its purely mathematical interpretation and instead understood it as a practical and existential act involving the subject’s transformation. Finally, this article shows how Miki reinterprets the wager as an existential transition grounded in what he calls “religious anxiety”. For Miki, the wager is not a logical proof of the existence of God but an act of the will through which the finite subject confronts its own finitude and opens itself to the infinite. In this way, the wager becomes a fundamental structure of human experience, in which anxiety is transformed into hope.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: La politique et la morale chez Montaigne et Pascal : le respect de la loi, même injuste, et l’aversion pour la réforme politique
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Politics and Morality in Montaigne and Pascal : Respect for the Law, Even When Unjust, and Aversion to Political Reform. We propose a comparative study of the political thought of Montaigne and Pascal, focusing on their shared insistence on respect for the law, even when it is unjust, and on their common distrust of political reform. An examination of textual parallels between the Essays and the Pensées highlights Pascal’s appropriation of Montaigne’s idea that laws derive their authority not from justice but from custom and usage. At the same time, it brings out Pascal’s own inflections, notably his emphasis on the role of imagination and on the political dangers involved in exposing the arbitrariness of laws. Finally, the convergence of the two authors in their aversion to political innovation is related to a theological justification of Augustinian inspiration, which subordinates political action to the preservation of civil peace.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Althusser lecteur de Pascal
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The article examines the extent to which Althusser’s theory of ideology, as formulated in the essay ‘Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses’, is indebted to Pascal. He illustrates two crucial aspects of the theory with reference to Pascal : first, the idea that material practices (such as religious rituals) actually bring about beliefs ; secondly, the idea that ideology involves ‘interpellation’—it sends a message to the individual about his or her duties, debts, and prospects. It is argued that the debt goes beyond this. Pascal argues that imagination (or opinion, a term he treats as effectively synonymous) plays a vital role in securing a social order produced by previous struggles between social groups, in which the winners secure their domination by instituting political and social structures and inculcating beliefs (opinions) that support these. These beliefs are inculcated through rituals which condition the bodies (and thus the beliefs) of both the dominant and the subordinate parties. It is argued that Althusser’s theory of ideology is effectively an adaptation of these views of Pascal’s to a Marxist theoretical context—a hypothesis brought out by what we know of Althusser’s youthful reading of the Pensées.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Écrire je
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article focuses on statements in the first person found in some of the books containing Pascal’s Pensées. Its aim is to use these statements as a starting point to contribute to the discussion about “how to do things with words” and, more specifically, to the debate on how this concept can be applied in historical analysis. The condition of the papers found upon Pascal’s death makes it impossible to seriously attempt to characterize the action that Pascal as an individual might have undertaken with the words written on these papers, which became the Pensées. In other words, it is illusory to speculate about an action other than the choice of these written words itself, other than this work that left fragments capable of all sorts of external interpretations of coherence. The Pensées exist, however, because Pascal’s contemporaries set about constructing their coherence: the fact that the distinction between the work of writing—the act of choosing words on paper—and the actions carried out with the writings that result from it has, in this instance, been preserved for us is part of the book’s critical strength. To outline the implications of this configuration, the presence of the first-person singular in the excerpts studied serves as a guide in the article.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Les caprices de Pascal
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Caprice, in the course of the seventeenth century, established itself as a complex and contested term in seventeenth-century French culture and society. The dictionary makers of the period distinguish between positive and negative meanings of the word. Furetière is typical in perceiving the word to have a negative meaning when it is applied to social behaviour that goes against all reasonable norms and in portraying caprice as potentially positive in its meaning when it is used to describe the flash of wit (génie) at the heart of artistic creativity. Louis Marin, in an important 1983 study of the concept, suggests that Pascal is the thinker of the period who articulates the transformation of caprice from a disorder of the imagination to a flash of creative wit. Yet – as this article shows – Pascal nowhere uses the term in that second, positive, sense. How is that absence best understood? As a random lexical effect or as the expression of a rhetorical strategy? In pursuit of the latter hypothesis, the article turns to Marin’s idea that Pascalian discourse produces a certain form of incompletion, using this idea to read anew the lexical presences and absences of caprice in the fabric of Pascal’s writings.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This contribution attempts to articulate two aspects of Pascal's thought that are generally perceived as being very far apart: on the one hand, his criticism of the practices of accommodatio (or adaptation to ritual contexts) in modern evangelization, particularly in China; on the other hand, his criticism of probabilism in the context of controversies over casuistry. oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Bourdieu et Pascal. Penser avec, ou Comment métaboliser un auteur ?
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article argues that Pierre Bourdieu’s Pascalian Meditations does not so much offer a commentary on Pascal as present a mode of thinking with him through the metabolization of his thought. What initially appears is an author-to-author relationship that presents itself as unmediated, notably remaining silent about its most plausible Marxist intermediaries (from Lefebvre to Goldmann). More fundamentally, however, Pascalian Meditations enacts a sociological actualization of Pascal, visible in the intertextual dialogue produced through Bourdieu’s notably loose practice of quotation, allusion, and reformulation. Pascal thus emerges as a tool for critical and reflexive inquiry, as a model for a praxeological approach capable of moving beyond the entrenched oppositions between objectivism and subjectivism, determinism and freedom. Bourdieu’s engagement with Pascal aims to promote the principle of the non-excluded middle, set against both the structuralist theory of rules and, by extension, “the Marxist vision of the centralized apparatus” and of mechanical alienation. Neither philological nor doctrinal, and characterized by processes of displacement and fluid absorption, Bourdieu’s claimed fidelity to Pascal is primarily pragmatic: it serves a struggle that is at once political and methodological—less as a means of asserting a position than as a means of clarification, understood here as a release from any overly simplistic framework.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In this powerful article, with his characteristic precise and penetrating style, our late friend constructs a concept of anomaly as “a significant irregularity behind apparent regularity,” which “persists in every ecosystem, [...] even those of the mind.” Echoing Pascal with references drawn mainly from the Bible and ecclesiastical history, but also from Durkheim, Livy, Nietzsche, and Döblin, he reveals anomaly (and the closely related concepts of syncope, aporia, and anomie) as the structuring principle of his writings, primarily the Pensées. oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The famous pensée on examples (Sellier 454) usually puzzles the reader with the false symmetry of these propositions: “When one wishes to demonstrate a general principle, one must provide the specific rule for a particular case. oai_dc:dc.dc:title: The Americanization of the French Social and Human Sciences? A Cartography of Translations from English, German, and Italian into French (2003–2013)
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Translating books is more significant for the international circulation of ideas within the social and human sciences than it is within the sciences. However, chances of a book being translated vary according to various factors: the centrality of original language, the symbolic capital of the author, and that of their publisher. This study of works in the social and human sciences translated into French between 2003 and 2013 reveals the state of unequal power relations between the three languages from which most of them originate: English, German, and Italian. The study shows that although the German tradition is still valued in the sub-field of the human and social sciences publishing in France, we are witnessing the virtual disappearance of contemporary German authors in favor of British and American researchers. This finding tends to confirm the idea of an American hegemony, which however needs to be relativized. The study of the authors of prefaces also reveals the different importation strategies of the cultural intermediaries (editors, literary agents) in this sub-field: economic, political, symbolic and academic.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Negotiating the Boundaries of the Speakable: The Introduction of Western Social and Human Sciences into the USSR by Progress Publishers (1963-1985)
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This paper examines the circulation of ideas and knowledge between Western countries and the Soviet Union through the translation of books in the social and human sciences. By analysing its internal structure and the socio-occupational trajectories of publishing managers, and reconstructing the academic networks associated with the publisher and its catalogues, this article reveals the logics that determined which books were imported, and examines the constraints on the production of translations in an authoritarian context.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the process of professionalization and autonomization of translation in the field of humanities and social sciences (HSS). This contribution is the result of a qualitative study based on interviews with professional translators specialised in HSS. The study is completed by observation, facilitated by the author’s professional position—as editorial assistant of HSS journals. A first part is about the low level of recognition of the HSS translation as an autonomous sector, both within the research community and regarding the other translation specialities. Academics, because of their specific internationalization strategies and the lack of funding, often bypass professional translation to favour self-translation or peer-translation. Between art and expertise, “literary” and “technical” translation, the HSS sector receives marginal attention from professional organizations dedicated to representing translators or scientific editors. Major technological innovations (neural machine translation and generative artificial intelligence) are intrinsically linked to organizational changes (notably the growth of translation agencies). Thus, digital transition highlights a low level of professional recognition which is an incentive for specialised translators—in particular the most qualified segment—to organize for the defense of their professional territory.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Une production symbolique du capitalisme responsable : le cas de l’huile de palme durable
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines so-called sustainable foods as a symbolic production of responsible capitalism. It focuses on the controversy surrounding the proposed taxation of palm oil in France between 2012 and 2016 (the “Nutella tax”). Initially introduced on political and public health grounds, the tax was gradually abandoned as a new narrative of “sustainable” palm oil took hold. Drawing on an analysis of parliamentary debates, communications from public and private actors, and a media corpus, the article shows how corporate lobbying and communication strategies redirected the issues at stake, turning a public health priority into a matter of sustainable development. Framing companies as competing for salvation rather than for profit enabled agri-food industries to continue their economic activity within a form of salvation capitalism, cast as serving the common good.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Being Your Own Chef. Are Digital Platforms a Professional Emancipation Vehicle for Expert Service Workers?
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the extent to which digital platforms are a professional emancipation vehicle for expert service workers providing personalized services. It focuses on the case of a personal chef platform to investigate its emancipatory effect for cooks seeking to escape the constraints of waged employment in the food service industry and entrepreneurship as a restaurateur. Drawing on interviews with twelve cooks and a platform manager as well as web scraping of the 283 chef profiles on the platform, the study analyses three aspects of emancipation: economic autonomy, existential autonomy (consisting of rethinking the place of work in life) and autonomy in the exercise of the work itself. The article shows that emancipation is incomplete. Earnings remain low, professional constraints are more reconfigured than eliminated, and new forms of subjection to customers and the platform can emerge.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Organisation du travail culinaire et consommation de produits ultratransformés
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In both expert and lay discourse, home cooking is seen as a rampart against unhealthy eating, as epitomized by ultraprocessed “industrial” foods. Culinary discourse of this kind contributes to the creation of symbolic frontiers of class and gender. In this article, we test the assumption upon which this discourse is based, i.e. that more time spent in the kitchen, by women in particular, is associated with lower ultraprocessed food consumption. Drawing on INSEE’s 2017 Household Budget survey (enquête Budget de famille), we focus on a sample of 3,210 couple households and use the NOVA nutritional definition of ultraprocessed foods. Our findings run counter to received ideas. Couples with the lowest incomes or educational levels are not the largest consumers of these products, and spending on ultraprocessed foods does not decrease when couples eat more home-cooked meals. While the youngest couples spend more on these foods, households with children, identified in the literature as the most receptive to messaging about healthy eating, are also large ultraprocessed food consumers.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Cooking and Art: A Field of Cultural Production under the Influence of the Market
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article addresses the relationship between professional culinary excellence and art. Whilst in existing scholarship philosophical approaches suppose an ontological link between these two categories and sociological research employs the concept of “artification,” my analysis is based on field theory. I consider cooking as a field of cultural production, which allows for the constructivist approach behind the legitimization of cooking to be translated through making use of the artistic comparison. The first part of the article demonstrates the extent to which cooking assumes the properties of fields of cultural production: a specific concern and a vocation discourse to succeed, recognition authorities led by peers and critics, a dynamic of disputes between avant-garde and consecrated chefs against the backdrop of permanent revolution. The second part addresses the specificities of the culinary field and, in particular, its lack of autonomy from the economic domain. This assessment leads to a broader reflection on the principles of distance between artistic fields and the market, in which I also interrogate the underlying principles of an economy of disinterestedness.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Borders, walls, and migrant characters who challenge them feature prominently in the works of Hugo Hamilton, a transnational author whose German mother immigrated to Ireland after World War 2. This article focuses on the depiction of the Berlin Wall in four of his novels set in Germany. Interweaving personal and world histories, past and present, Hamilton explores relationships – with places as much as with people. In Surrogate City (1990), the narrative focuses on the character of Helen who has moved from Ireland to West Berlin, while the characters in The Love Test (1995) are from East Berlin and attempt to cross over to flee the Stasi. The protagonist of Disguise (2008) is in and out of Berlin in search of his own story and history. In Every Single Minute (2014), the narrator Liam takes his dying friend on a last touristic trip to the German capital. The corpus offers four different perspectives on the Berlin Wall that span a little over a decade in terms of publication, but nearly forty years with regards to the narratives: Surrogate City is set during the Cold War, The Love Test and Disguise alternate between chapters in a post-war, partitioned Germany and passages set in the aftermath of 1989, while Every Single Minute takes place in contemporary times. This study focuses on the depiction and significance of the Berlin Wall in the novels, from its historical role as a boundary between two worldviews, separating people, to its fall and the aftermath of it. The chronology of the novels reflects that of the Wall’s history and affects its depiction in the narratives. This geocritical study examines the fictional representation of a geographical place and the evolution of this portrayal. Simultaneously, the article argues for the use of sensorial mapping in literary analysis. Exemplifying it through the study of Hamilton’s novels, a case is made for this cartographical practice that subverts the conventions of the discipline in order to highlight emotions and impressions, making it all the more suited to literary geography and geocriticism. Maps are thus included to illustrate and reinforce the points made in this study, further challenging the boundaries between disciplines.
