oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Anomalous Borders, Geographical Knowledge, and the Inner Line in India
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the Inner Line system in British India’s northeastern frontier to show how borders are historically produced and dynamic. Introduced through the Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation of 1873, the Inner Line operated as an internal administrative partition that nonetheless functioned as the practical limit of sovereign authority in a region where the external border remained undefined until 1914. What existed beyond the Inner Line, therefore, was a zone where sovereignty was fragmented and where law remained mired in ambiguity.Over time, the Inner Line was repeatedly redefined, becoming a key element of colonial governance in the region – all the while remaining indefinite, almost by design. It enabled extra-legal colonial interventions and institutionalised a civilizational distinction between the hill and valley populations. The article traces various spatial and ethnological discourses that framed the hills as an unruly frontier. This representation underpinned the Inner Line and was developed over the 19th and 20th centuries through surveying, mapping and ethnological classification to naturalise a new colonial territorial order. It argues that the line was not just a geographical division but a mechanism that reshaped the region’s patterns of mobility and association to fit within the imperial economic and administrative order. Previous studies on northeastern India have analysed how colonial interventions framed the region’s geography, agrarian structure, and security concerns. This article builds on such scholarship, situating the Inner Line within wider discussions on frontiers in British India. By tracing how the Line was repeatedly redrawn, amended, and circumvented, the article emphasises its fluidity and its role as a flexible technology of power that regulated mobility, economic extraction, and administrative reach. Finally, I show how, in post‑colonial India, the Inner Line has acquired new and often competing meanings — becoming at once a security instrument, a mechanism of indigenous protection, and a site of political contestation.

This shifts the attention away from efforts to securitise natural borders and instead exposes their potential for fostering solidarity between nations as well generating more inclusive visions of national belonging.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: On the Borders of the Imaginary, “Erring” on the Side of Hope: Western Mapping, Exploration and the Jeffersonian Design
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Christopher Columbus and James Cook both share similar features—one of them is to have failed to discover what made up the actual purpose of their quests; they did, however, “f[i]nd what they wanted to see,” as reflected in the writings and maps the two illustrious explorers handed over to posterity. This assumption by Thomas P. Slaughter appears to also fully apply to Meriwether Lewis and William Clark, sent by Thomas Jefferson beyond the frontier, in search of the legendary Northwest Passage, a hypothetical transcontinental water route the control of which would promote the implementation of the expansionist design. While the enterprise itself—among other objectives—aimed at furthering cartographic knowledge, the prospect of exploration also required to be fully acquainted with the region to be traveled, ahead of the journey. Jefferson had succeeded in gathering precious data but the mental image still remained very much incomplete: his judgment was flawed with regard to the actual distances and hardships of the project, which might never have taken shape, had the fictitious map not temporarily supplanted the true reality of frontier geography. Challenged throughout the “wilderness” experience, the heralds of Jeffersonianism quickly measured the gap between the mental construct and actual daily life within an unconquerable natural environment that put the Western cartographers under heavy strain, even undermining their methodology. The travelers also took particular care in collecting the invaluable information provided by the Natives—whose perfect mastery of the territory had been granted to them by the thousands of years during which they had been occupying the place—only to find out that the Native American approach to cartography usually mirrors Indigenous thinking more than it helps deepen the “civilized” man’s understanding of the spatio-temporal framework he progresses in. In this respect, beside merely representing space, maps might also be construed as the subjective projection of the mind they spring from.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: How Donald Trump’s intentional mispronunciations of Kamala Harris’s first name support the hypothesis that loanwords exhibit distinct phonological properties
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This study shows how Donald Trump, by intentionally mispronouncing the first name of his opponent in the 2024 presidential election, Kamala Harris, supports the theory that the English lexicon is composed of subsystems. The words which belong to one subsystem share linguistic properties that distinguish them from the items of the other subsystems. Each subsystem arises from the interaction of specific phonetic, phonological, letter-to-sound, morphological, segmental, syntactic, semantic, and frequency-related properties, which makes it possible to distinguish the subsystems from each other. Native English speakers are sensitive to the different properties of sublexica and in particular to those of loanwords which are grouped in the §Foreign subsystem. The words of the §Foreign subsystem balance conforming to English-system principles with maintaining their own distinct features, as they often retain some properties of the source languages. This conflict gives them a specific status in English, especially from the point of view of pronunciation. By intentionally pronouncing Kamala Harris’s first name with phonetic and phonological principles that are typically attested in the words of foreign origin and which are detailed in the article (location of primary stress, pronunciation of stressed vowels with a “foreign value” and absence of vowel reduction in unstressed contexts), Donald Trump, as a political strategist, points to Kamala Harris’s origin and, by doing so, attempts to discredit the Democratic candidate in the eyes of the American electorate.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Restoring Wonder: Mystical Counter-Mapping in the Work of Arthur Machen
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The Welsh writer Arthur Machen (1863-1947) is now widely recognized as a literary precursor of psychogeography, both as a way of walking and as a study of the interaction between geography and psychology. Like their creator, many of his characters practise what Machen called “the art of wandering”, an art not unlike the situationist dérive in that it liberates the walker from the alienation of the everyday.This article explores Machen’s London writing, both fictional and non-fictional, to show how it ties in with his mystical agenda as a writer. The author and his fictional mouthpieces consistently voice their dislike of the disenchanted, de-spiritualized world they live in. As they participate in the disenchantment of space, maps and guidebooks are rejected in an explicit anti-map discourse. Furthermore, maps cannot render the porosity of space as perceived by the mystically inclined, for whom gateways into the unknown might appear almost anywhere. I argue that the reshaping of London in Machen’s work is an act of counter-mapping in that it opposes what Peter Ackroyd describes as “a secular view of the world”.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: A Performative Intermedial Analysis of The Willow Song
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This study offers a performative intermedial analysis of The Willow Song in Shakespeare’s Othello, examining how lyrics and music interact as mutually shaping media and how this multimodal relationship contributes to the play’s emotional, symbolic, and educational resonance. Building on theories of embodied cognition and multimodal learning, the article conceptualises intermedial analysis as an approach that integrates literary and musicological perspectives through the act of performing the song, thereby foregrounding aesthetic, affective, and experiential dimensions often overlooked in strictly textual readings. The Willow Song, introduced in the 1623 Folio version of Othello, emerges as a culturally stratified artefact rooted in Renaissance melancholy traditions, where the willow symbolised sorrow and abandoned love. Its appearance in Act IV, Scene 3—sung by Desdemona in an intimate domestic exchange with Emilia—functions as a lyrical and emotional counterpoint to the brutal logic of toxic masculinity, racial prejudice, and patriarchal violence that drives the tragedy toward its catastrophic end. The article contextualises the song within the broader narrative structure of Othello, exploring themes of racism, xenophobia, and femicide that remain profoundly resonant in contemporary society. Drawing on historical and critical sources, the study traces how Shakespeare reworked earlier narratives to address the contradictions of Elizabethan London—a city characterised by social hierarchy, mercantile expansion, and growing ethnic diversity. The contribution underlines how musicality permeates Shakespeare’s dramaturgy, presenting a detailed intermedial analysis of The Willow Song, based on an archival transcription consulted at the Barbican Centre Music Library. The analysis examines melodic contour, modal inflections, rhetorical figures, prosody, phonetic patterns, and their articulation with lyrical content. Features such as descending fifths, modal shifts between Aeolian, Dorian, and major inflections, repeated motifs, and rhetorical devices like hypotyposis contribute to the song’s haunting emotional effect. The lyrics amplify this musical expressiveness through alliteration, sibilance, consonance, assonance, personification, and symbolic imagery, producing a refined sonic texture that mirrors the play’s thematic concerns. The article concludes by highlighting the educational potential of intermedial approaches to Shakespeare. In a sociocultural context marked by declining engagement with literary classics and increasing educational fragmentation, music-literature laboratories offer valuable opportunities for multimodal and multisensory learning. By integrating performance, analysis, and embodied interpretation, The Willow Song can serve as an entry point for students—particularly non-native speakers—to engage critically with Shakespeare’s texts, fostering inclusive participation and creative inquiry.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Claiming Space: Aboriginal (Re)mappings of Contemporary Australia
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Contemporary Indigenous-authored texts are often read as counter-narratives seeking to redress erroneous and oppressive representations of themselves in white-authored texts. Similarly, Indigenous narratives concerned with place and reclaiming the land lost to colonisation can be read as counter-mapping exercises, insofar as they engage not only with representations of space and the territory itself, but also question the very legitimacy of colonial cartography and therefore settler presence and ways of constructing knowledge about place. This paper engages with the Australian Aboriginal notion of “country” and its relationship with language, particularly in Alexis Wright’s 2006 award-winning novel Carpentaria, set in the eponymous Gulf of Carpentaria in far-north Queensland. Carpentaria tells the story of the Aboriginal Pricklebush people and their relationship with Uptown, the white zone of the fictional town of Desperance, and the Gurrfurrit mine. I argue that Wright is concerned with the way language is used in contemporary Australia to (re)inscribe Aboriginal presence onto the land and overwrite colonial inscriptions through the renaming of colonised places, the articulation of spiritual spaces such as the Dreaming, as well as the remapping of Indigenous bodies and languages as textual spaces. Indeed, Aboriginal writing itself can be likened to a frontier zone along which lies, on one side of the border, literacy, theory, materiality, and history; and on the other side, orality, experience, performance, and myth. Beyond stereotypical binaries, Wright writes from this frontier zone that blurs the border between the margin and centre of postcolonial discourse and complicates the position of the white reader in relation to space(s). Drawing from postcolonial theories of language, territory, and embodiment, I examine how Wright addresses the tensions between local traditions and rampant globalisation to illustrate the ongoing struggle for Indigenous mapping systems to overwrite external and internal colonial cartography, from natural features such as rivers in the Gulf, to sacred spaces like the Dreaming, and even the inner landscape of the reader who attempts to situate themselves within the story and orientate themselves with Wright’s words. As a response to colonial cartography, I examine “unsettlement” as particularly apt to describe the contemporary thrust of Aboriginal writing in Australia, where the very legitimacy of the settler state is threatened by official acknowledgements of the illegality of colonisation, as well as previous and ongoing ownership of the land by Indigenous people.

It therefore calls for a nuanced sociological analysis of irrigation management, one that takes into account rural restructuring, visions of development, and the legacy of struggles for fairer water management.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Occitanie : l’envers démographique d’une région attractive
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Occitanie, a dynamic region in southwestern Europe, stands out for its strong demographic appeal driven by its two metropolitan areas and its Mediterranean coastline. Yet this image conceals a more contrasted reality, as two-thirds of the region consist of sparsely populated rural areas characterized by pronounced demographic ageing, the decline of public services, and persistent socio-economic vulnerabilities. Based on research conducted between 2023 and 2025 in partnership with the Grands Causses Regional Natural Park in the Aveyron’s department, this article examines the demographic trajectories of so-called “low-density” areas in this department and, more broadly, across the regional scale. Drawing on diachronic demographic data, the INSEE typological framework, and insights from interviews with local officials, civil servants, and planners, it highlights the territorial reconfigurations driven by residential mobility, metropolitan influence, and spatial planning policies. While the much-discussed “rural renaissance” in the aftermath of the 2020 health crisis remains scarcely observable, several future scenarios emerge: inertia and declining attractiveness, the valorization of ecological and productive resources, or strategic digital reconfigurations through teleworking, smart villages, and the relocalization of certain functions. Ultimately, what is at stake here is not the unequal distribution of population in Occitanie but the very nature of the so-called “empty spaces” Far from any homogeneous or deterministic vision, the article argues for a nuanced and contextualized reading of rural dynamics, where low density does not equate to emptiness or the absence of projects, but rather calls for a rethinking of public policies at the scale of local territories.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Are sparsely populated areas more disconnected from local labor markets? Examining local migration intensities in northern Sweden
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Sparsely populated areas (SPAs) have recently been described as a special geographic category with a range of unique features. One such feature is the idea that individual settlements are disconnected from each other (internally disconnected), and becoming increasingly disconnected over time, as they are separated by distance, diverse development pathways and different socio-economic characteristics. SPAs lack the sorts of stable and reciprocal core-periphery structures common for rural areas in more densely populated settings, meaning that they do not share populations and labor markets within their regions and rely on external and more unpredictable sources of human capital. This paper examines the extent to which the disconnectedness hypothesis applies in the context of sparsely populated municipalities in northern Sweden. Specifically, it compares local (within-county) migration intensities of working age people in northern SPAs with those in other Swedish municipalities over a 21-year period, considering differences across age groups. It also analyses the relationships between change in migration intensity, net-migration position, and population growth over time. The results confirm that northern SPAs were more disconnected than the rest of Sweden, particularly when looking at in-migration intensity. However, they were not consistently more disconnected than other rural municipalities in the south, raising questions about the validity of disconnectedness as an independently defining feature of SPAs. We also find that increased connectedness (through higher local migration intensities) leads to lower in-migration rates for most age groups and poorer net-migration position, suggesting that more resource intensive external labor recruitment may have more desirable outcomes than local labor development.

Bringing together sociology, geography, anthropology and history, the analysis is based on a body of qualitative and quantitative data (archives, semi-structured interviews, institutional statistics). The current discourses relating to the isolation of the Cerdagne and the Haut-Conflent are compared with historical dynamics. The analysis reveals a distortion between the register of isolation used by the actors to characterize this territory and the demographic, economic and cultural dynamics that animate it for a long time. This cross-border space connects people more than it separates them. The feeling of isolation expressed by the inhabitants is induced by the withdrawal of services and shops or their tourist specialization increased since the 30 glorious. If the urban-centered reference of a breakaway by the (auto)road connection is still visible in the collected speeches, it tends to give way to chosen immobility.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Since the 19th century, the gradual development of tourism in mountain regions has led to differentiated spatial development. However, the declining availability of snow (re)calls into question the long-term sustainability of this model (Marcelpoil and François, 2008). Beyond these economic centers (ski resorts), less-developed mountain areas are highly heterogeneous, shaped by varying forms of regulation (such as nature reserves, regional or national parks, and communal lands) and by a wide range of human activities, both professional and recreational. Mountain huts provide a valuable lens through which to understand the social and spatial dynamics at play in these areas. Based on the study of huts, this article explores the specific characteristics of these spaces and the different forms of human activity they host. Work, recreational practices, and governance structures are influenced by the specific features of less-developed mountain areas, while also contributing to characterizing them.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: De l’épure à la modélisation informatique avancée. Le rapport au savoir mathématique dans la conception graphique des formes architecturales
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Technical drawing for the design and construction of buildings — of which the hand sketch for construction is the purest expression — has undergone a long evolution of rationalizations before reaching a level of coherence, efficiency and scientific validity. As a graphic tool inextricably linked to geometry, it bends the iconic to the rigor of mathematics. Especially when it comes to designing relatively complex architectural forms, graphic techniques, particularly those stemming from Monge's descriptive geometry, guide the way formal generation is conceived, impose a specific relationship to mathematical knowledge, and condition the geometric typologies used or even invented. Advanced computer tools, which mobilize mathematical models inaccessible to the average architect, radically alter this relationship to scientific knowledge and, consequently, the ways in which architectural forms are conceived and designed. They also implicitly change the role of the image itself in the design process.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Idéation architecturale et intelligence artificielle : une étude sur le statut des images générées et l’intentionnalité des architectes
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Images play a key role in architectural practice. They are produced and used to inspire, understand, project, communicate, and even catalogue architectural projects. Recent developments in AI-based image generation systems (AIIGS) and their widespread accessibility have enabled their adoption by architects and architecture students. One of their main uses in architecture is to stimulate designers’ creativity during the ideation phase (emergence of ideas). This paper offers a theoretical reflection alongside an exploratory study, conducted in an educational setting and aimed at observing the “ideation pathways” of students assisted by AIIGS. The study thus seeks to explore the impact of using AIIGS in architectural ideation, and the status attributed to generated images within the ideation process. The idea that AIIGS might enable designers to “make discoveries through serendipity” proved limited in the experiment. Once designers committed to a line of inquiry, they generally rejected generated images that diverged from their initial design intentions. We also observed that the way initial project intentions were developed (through sketches or reference images) had a strong influence on how AIIGS were used. To identify the status designers assign to generated images, we proposed distinguishing several functions: idea-images (to inspire), analogon-images (to explore solutions), and model-images (to communicate the project). The results suggest that designers primarily attribute an analogon-image status to generated images; that is, they are seen as intermediate steps for exploring solutions, going beyond the simple role of “reference images” they are often assigned. The article thus opens up avenues for reflection on how AIIGS may shape architectural ideation.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Entre terrain et orbite : articuler images satellitaires et photographie située pour comprendre les Alpes occitanes

In response to the obsolescence of models of the ‘idealised mountain’, the research explores the tension between the bird’s-eye view offered by digital tools and the situated experience of photographic surveying. Focusing on the Val Vermenagna, an observatory of socio-economic changes between France and Italy, the article presents an experimental system of multiscale representation. Rather than treating digital and analogue images as in opposition, the study integrates them within a dynamic overlay platform. This protocol brings the metric precision of geospatial data into dialogue with the phenomenological depth of field experience.The methodology thus proposes an epistemological shift: moving from an aerial perspective to an embodied survey, where digital tools serve as preliminary mapping instruments that are ultimately grounded in the physical dimension of the place. The aim is to define new representation protocols capable of making intelligible landscapes of uncertainty and to rethink contemporary modes of mountain inhabitation.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: L’Architecte face à la boîte noire
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the instrumentation of architectural design processes in the digital age, placing the question of the image and its transformations at the center of the discussion. It is based on the hypothesis that every project originates from a mental image, which the architect seeks to translate into reality through a series of mediations. This translation is not a simple passage from idea to form, but rather a set of transformations operating within black boxes, understood as systems whose inputs and outputs are identifiable, while their internal logics are opaque. Within this framework, the article proposes to move beyond the opposition between traditional drawing and digital imagery by describing design as a dynamic process of circulation and transformation of images. For the architect, the mental image unfolds between a projected image, that which intention manages to formulate, and a perceived image, that which is interpreted in return. From the machine’s perspective, the image is configured between a thought image, that which can effectively be transmitted to a computer, and a visualized thought, that which is made visible on the screen. Design thus appears as a space of negotiation between these four instances, the coherence of which conditions the act of projecting. The introduction of digital tools and computer-generated imagery is not merely a change of medium, but profoundly transforms the very conditions of architectural thinking. These technical devices orient, filter, and shape design gestures, leading to formatting phenomena through which the projected image tends to adjust to the constraints of the thought image; that is, to the translation capacities offered by digital systems. The risk is thus one of homogenization of production, where form follows the implicit logics of the tools. To analyze this reconfiguration, the article proposes a taxonomy of design postures—user, gamer, maker, and hacker—describing different ways of articulating black boxes and the relationships between intention, perception, and generation. This classification highlights a shift in the role of the architect, who can no longer be understood solely as an author, but rather as a mediator within a sociotechnical network composed of both human and non-human actors. Ultimately, the article argues that the contemporary challenge is not to fully eliminate the opacity of these systems, but to develop a technical culture that enables their understanding, manipulation, and appropriation. Only on this basis may architects avoid alienation and reassert a critical capacity in relation to these tools.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Entre la main et l’image générative : la conception architecturale bouleversée par l’essor de l’IA ?
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article aims to advance understandings of AI-induced professional transformations in architecture, based on a case study of the French architecture agency AREP. Conducted in the summer of 2025, the study explores the agency’s integration of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) into image production practices during architectural design. The methodology draws on qualitative interviews with six professionals, representing various postures regarding this emerging technology. The results revealed two main attitudes in relation to AI and GAI: enthusiasts and sceptics. Four distinct profiles were further identified, providing fruitful insight regarding creative authorship, the potential erosion of image-related skills, and the risk of diminished expertise, while also outlining diverse work strategies in response to these tools. While GAI appears to be consolidating its role as a tool for inspiration and idea generation, its status remains ambiguous in a profession where human expertise—especially its sensory and tacit dimensions—remains fundamental. More broadly, the introduction of these new tools raises questions about the nature of the profession, potentially acting to reveal the architect’s role by forcing a reflection on the “non-verbalizable” aspects of architecture.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Muter sous la contrainte : les images numériques comme traducteurs de phénomènes invisibles et initiateurs de nouvelles pratiques
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Since the first computer-aided design programs in the 1960s, digital technology has profoundly transformed architectural tools and modes of representation. Today, it accompanies every stage of a project, generating a multitude of digital images along the way: analytical, technical, inspirational, among others. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has redefined the very nature of some of these images, as it is now capable of formulating design proposals and directly influencing the design process. At the same time, digital technology, through the images it produces, renders previously invisible phenomena visible—forces, flows, pollution, etc.—positioning these images as mediators between data, representations, and projects. Practices such as those of Forensic Architecture demonstrate how these images can also acquire critical and political value. Others, like prospective-architecture.fr, explore the operational potential of such images in the project’s creative process. This interactive digital tool for the design of low-carbon regional architecture enables the dynamic visualization of both the cost and environmental impact of a project throughout its development, thereby supporting conceptual, economic, and environmental trade-offs in alignment with the architectural quality of the resulting designs. These new articulations between data, representation, and production are now transforming architectural design and giving rise to new modes of production. However, in the face of the climate crisis, the proliferation of digital images must be examined in relation to their environmental footprint. Digital images are thus increasingly established as integral tools within the production process, situated at the intersection of technological, ethical, and ecological concerns.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: De l’atlas au dataset. Notes sur une imagination architecturale artificielle et étendue
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: For architects, collecting and organising images represents a form of externalisation of the process by which their imagination is constructed. This article sets out to explore how AI-generated images may constitute a further evolution of this process. It draws on the extended mind theory developed by philosophers Andy Clark and David Chalmers, recently updated by Clark to suggest that large language model (LLM)-based AI systems may externalise human cognitive faculties. It examines the extent to which architectural images produced by generative adversarial networks (GAN) and diffusion models—capable of generating new images from large datasets—might contribute to the ecology of the externalisation of architectural imagination. Through the lens of visual culture, the article analyses the types of AI-generated architectural images currently circulating, focusing on case studies from the French context. Two main categories are identified in particular: photorealistic depictions of feasible buildings, and unrealistic or unbuildable ones. It then outlines potential scenarios—both negative and positive—that these two types of images could open up for architectural imagination, considered through the framework of the extended mind.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Migrazioni situate, percorsi alternativi
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: There are several biases that weigh on migration studies, including the tendency to think of foreign “communities” as monolithic and homogeneous and the reduced analysis of their segmentations, especially in the context of long-term rooting processes. These limitations are even more evident in a context such as the Italian one, where immigrant communities have taken on specific forms and characteristics depending on the local context in which they have settled. The study therefore uses the perspective of migratory stratifications to investigate how the Tunisian communities of Modena and Ragusa have entered their respective contexts and how the relationship between territory and community has impacted the permeability of the latter with respect to new arrivals and their political-associative structuring. Based on 45 interviews with first-generation migrants and 20 with key informants, the study explores the diversities of these immigrant communities, linking them to the peculiar migratory stratification that they feed and in which they are inserted.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In this article I analyse the history of migration policies in the UK as focusing in different moments on colonial, EU, and qualified migrations. oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The 2024 European elections took place against a backdrop of significant political, economic, and social transformations. This paper offers a comparative reflection on electoral participation across the Member States of the European Union, with the aim of identifying recurring patterns within national contexts. Specifically, it explores how voter turnout is distributed in relation to certain structural socio-economic and cultural characteristics, adopting an ecological perspective. The analysis reveals the presence of relatively homogeneous profiles, while also highlighting internal differences that appear to reflect the role of institutional and political specificities. The findings point to the value of a multidimensional approach to participation, one that integrates material resources, cultural factors, and mobilization dynamics. The goal is to provide an empirical basis for understanding current trends in political participation in Europe, contributing to the broader debate on democratic quality and voting dynamics in diverse contexts.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Verso una congiunzione funzionale delle due “etiche” weberiane
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In the final pages of his Politik als Beruf, Max Weber introduced his now widely known and cited distinction between two types of ethics, i.e. the seemingly dichotomous relationship between the “ethics of conviction” (gesinnungsethik) and the “ethics of responsibility” (verantwortungsethik). This proposal has provoked widespread reaction, strong endorsement and quite favorable comments as well as a significant amount of criticism. The purpose of this article, however, is exactly to avoid such hypostatized interpretations of Weber’s work, trying instead to envision a sort of functional integration of the two kinds of ethics, making the case for a blurred and nuanced reading of this famous socio-political pair of concepts. Under this light, Weber’s distinction is best understood as a differentiation between analytical models and not ontological entities – actually, the two ethics seem to be inexorably intertwined with one another, in a constant play of juxtapositions and mutual cross-references.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: “Socioanalisi”: primi elementi per una riformulazione della teoria sociale come analisi critica della sociazione
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Starting from deep-rooted crisis of contemporary social sciences, we need to reformulate our theoretical approach in order to enhancing interpretative knowledge of our social realities. The first step of this analytic program is to deconstruct the historical paradigm of “critical theory” as a hypostatic way to explain social reality in its totality. From this perspective I propose a passage from “critical theory” to “socioanalysis” seen as an analytical-descriptive process without standardization. From this point of view the analysis of sociation (socioanalysis on the analogy of psychoanalysis) is always a critical approach to social reality because its explicative frame is not “prescriptive” but only “possible” (that is polyvalent). In this analytical context we have to confront with concept of ambivalence. This means that “things are in one way but they also are in another way”: existence, social life, interaction, agency, thought cannot be unequivocally interpreted. From this point of view I discuss two examples of contemporary theories that are implicitly ambivalent: the non-critical theory of Bruno Latour and the pragmatic theory of criticism of Luc Boltanski.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Robert K. Merton e il software libero: gli imperativi istituzionali della ricerca scientifica nell’etica hacker
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Free (and open source) software can be considered a sort of «total social phenomenon» in contemporary information society: it includes elements pertaining to the cultural, organizational and economical sphere and many others. Despite the fact that it is still often thought of as a «new» phenomenon, the model of production and diffusion of free software incorporates basic principles that have characterized modern western science since at least five centuries. In particular, the sociologist of science Robert K. Merton, in a famous essay of 1942, has formulated the institutional norms that every scientist will learn in the course of his education and that he will have to observe to gain respect and reputation within the community of his peers. These same norms (universalism, communism, disinterestedness and organised skepticism) perfectly depict the processes of production and diffusion of free software. We can therefore conclude that it is proprietary software (and not free software) that represents a historical anomaly in the models of production and organization of knowledge.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Sociologia del terrorismo iracheno: un’analisi di Al-Qaeda in Iraq
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The article analyses one of the most radical examples in the contemporary terrorism – the campaign of Al-Qaeda in Iraq since the 2003 invasion by the US-led coalition. Once specified the role of Al-Qaeda in Iraq within the Iraqi insurgency, the text offers an explanation of its development and strengthening up to the first half of 2008 – by indentifying its political objective, its capacity of exploiting specific political and social opportunities after the overthrow of Saddam Hussein, its strategy and tactics, with special reference to the heavy resort to terrorist attacks. On this basis, it is underlined the fact that Al-Qaeda in Iraq is part of the transnational network of Al-Qaeda because of at least three features: the struggle for the liberation of Muslim countries from the occupation of the US and its allies; a revolutionary campaign against the secular regimes which govern the Islamic world and, conjointly, a vigilant action in opposition to the growing power of the Shiites; e, finally, a systematic use of the most extreme methods of asymmetric warfare, in particular the indiscriminate suicide attacks on civilians.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: I criteri di valutazione della desiderabilità sociale delle occupazioni
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In this paper we study the evaluation criteria used by individuals to rank occupations according to their social desirability. We use qualitative and quantitative data from the recent national study «The social evaluation of occupations in Italy».The process of evaluating occupations has a multidimensional nature. Interviewees adopt not only traditional criteria but also a series of new elements peculiar to the current Italian social and economic system. They also introduce some issues, such as the gender of the person who performs an occupation, the type of contract and the place of employment. The hierarchies behind the evaluation criteria seem to be shared by the majority of the interviewees and they also seem to be relatively constant over time. The emphasis given to each criterion, or to the underlying social construct, tends to vary in a structured way amongst interviewees. Considerations on the use of the stratification scales and on the relative methodological implications are drawn.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Conoscenza tacita e argomentazione retorica nei modelli di simulazione sociale
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The process of defining representations of computational simulation models in the social sciences is not only logical, but also interpretative, in that the “tacit knowledge” of Polanyi (1966) and also rhetoric – the knowledge of “how we speak” and “how we write” – come into play.Within the social sciences, the relationship between the data of a simulation, on the one hand, and the empirical facts, on the other, remains a problem with no easy solution. Many social scientists who make use of simulation maintain that its principal role is that of a tool that is capable of constructing and testing social theories. To better understand this role, therefore, we need to define what is meant by the term “scientific theory”. There are, essentially, two types of scientific theory that are constructed and tested by means of simulation models: 1) systems of propositions that interpret, in some particular way, a set of empirical facts; 2) systems of propositions depending on an interpretation by way of an analogy derived from a different scientific field.This paper analyses, for each type of theory, what rhetorical strategies the authors of the simulation models use, and what is the “tacit knowledge” they based upon.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: La partecipazione elettorale in Italia
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The aim of the paper is to analyze electoral participation in Italy against the decline in turnout in elections during the Second Republic. Each election yields a variable proportion of citizens not taking part in the vote. In order to measure this phenomenon accurately, we first need to define the non-voter turnout by considering abstention, null and blank votes considered as components of electoral not participation. Successively we show the geographical distribution of uninvolved people underlying the dualism North and South and the differences between first-order and second-order elections in the level of turnout. In the final part of the article we claim that abstention is really only one dimension of a more general process of instability in voting behavior. We identify electoral volatility, partisan identification and vote to protest parties as further evidence in order to state a specific syndrome of declining legitimacy for main actors in democracy loosing the grip with electorate.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: La relation entre tradition/transmission et créativité à travers une ethnographie des oka no mochi
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This paper presents an ethnography of the custom of offering rice cakes to the deity Oka no kami during New Year in a village in Akita. It examines how these practices are perceived by the actors involved, taking into account their lifeworld –that is, reality as it is subjectively experienced by them– and thus seeks to develop a notion of denshō (transmission/tradition) grounded in the reality of observed customs. Rather than reducing tradition to mere inheritance, the article adopts both diachronic and synchronic perspectives to account for the dynamism of practices as lived within communities, and conceptualizes transmission as a multi-layered process in which each actor contributes to its reconfiguration.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Sur les traces des dragons du musée Cernuschi : étude de la frise sculptée (miyabori) d’un temple japonais
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: In 2023, the Cernuschi Museum in Paris restored a masterpiece from its original collection: an ornamental sculpture (miyabori) of extraordinary dimensions. Representing three dragons, the sculpture is believed to have come from a Japanese Buddhist temple. From the start of the restoration, our team has been working to retrace the journey of the sculpture, from its creation in Japan to its arrival in Paris. Our investigation evolved by combining archival research, motif studies, anatomical analyses of the wood, and traditional and digital morphological comparisons of a large corpus of miyabori. This research opens new horizons for determining the connections between miyabori and the artisan-sculptors who created them.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: « Écrire » l’élève dans le Japon du début du xxe siècle : le rôle des carnets de correspondance
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The report cards kept by Japanese pupils during the first half of the 20th century provide valuable written evidence of how education was subordinated to the nationalist and imperialist aims of the state. The Ministry of Education played a central role in shaping a disciplined and homogeneous “Japanese body”. This is most notable in the continuous monitoring in schools of students’ physical development, behaviour, and academic performance – practices documented in these cards. The cards also reveal the tensions within the school system, which was torn between the twofold role assigned to assessment: a tool of standardisation serving the state’s project, and a ruthless mechanism for selecting future secondary school students.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This paper explores the temporalities at play in the recent revitalisation of wooden barrel use within the fermentation culture of contemporary Japan. More than a decade ago, a group of soy sauce brewers and carpenters initiated a revival project aimed at protecting endangered brewing techniques and passing on “the authentic taste” of soy sauce to future generations. This article draws on ethnographic research with members of that project as they engage in numerous activities and events. It shows that the brewers are less concerned with the reinvention of an idealised past than they are with crafting the (uncertain) futures of wooden barrel soy sauce.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Les débats autour de l’interdiction des femmes dans les lieux sacrés à la suite de l’incident de Maizuru (avril 2018)
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: The Maizuru incident of 2018 sparked controversy when female medics who were attending a government official suffering a cardiac arrest were ordered to leave the sacred area of the sumo arena. It highlighted the issue of nyonin kinsei – the prohibition of women from entering sacred spaces. Covered extensively by the media, the incident pitted the defense of “tradition” against the denunciation of gender discrimination, with many observers arguing that the idea of nyonin kinsei is incompatible with contemporary notions of equality. Researchers point to the constructed nature of such prohibition, which are often “traditions” created retrospectively in the modern era. This episode thus illustrates the tension between inherited religious practices and current social norms. It also reveals the potential for change as society evolves demographically and as women continue to play a more prominent role in rituals and ceremony.

oai_dc:dc.dc:title: Les jardins de Claude Monet : trajectoires de la tradition paysagère entre la France et le Japon
oai_dc:dc.dc:description: Through an analysis of Claude Monet’s turn of the 20th century Giverny garden, this article reflects on the influence of Japonism in its landscape design and the subsequent transposition of that design to contemporary Japan. Although the garden at Giverny should not be understood simply as a Japanese garden built overseas, the Japanese bridge, wisteria and water lilies form a picture heavily influenced by images of the Land of the Rising Sun. Those images were also central to the restoration work performed on the garden in the 1970s. Today, the image of the garden is widely reproduced in Japan, not in its entirety, but more often in smaller snapshots selected for their aesthetic qualities. An understanding of the spatial composition of the garden therefore recedes in favour of these smaller pictorial motifs, which in turn are transposed throughout the Japanese archipelago, much like the prints of famous places once displayed in pre-modern gardens.

oai_dc:dc.dc:description: This article examines the notion of tradition associated with the world of Japanese sweets, wagashi. The first part sheds light on the mechanisms involved in the historical development of this culinary tradition. Then, to better understand its contemporary issues, several confectionery shops located outside major metropolitan areas are presented, illustrating strategies of creativity developed in response to challenging economic conditions. Finally, the heritage-making (patrimonialization) of wagashi within the broader context of tourism development highlights their increasingly central role in both local and national cultural policies.
